title: The Insurance Industry
objectives: Guide clients through the different types of non-government insurers operating throughout Canada.
Explain the different kinds of insurance delivery systems used for life and property/liability insurance.
Explain to clients the regulation (both government and industry self-regulation) of the insurance industry in Canada.
Help clients understand the various types of government-run (federal and provincial) insurance programs.

guide.heading: How the insurance industry evolved
points: Early years: formal separation by type of risk. Each company covered one specific risk, such as fire or marine transportation.

Today coverage has melded into four broad categories: property, liability, accident and sickness, and life. A homeowner's policy, for example, covers fire, theft, vandalism and burst pipes, plus contents, alternative lodging and liability.

Regulators still try to keep the life sector separate from the property and liability sector. Many full-line insurers exist, and some large groups use a holding company to own a life company and a P&L company under one umbrella.
The industry's two major sectors: life, annuity and disability; and property and liability.
Non-government insurers match supply to demand through pricing (premiums). Government provides coverage where they do not, generally because the risks fail the criteria for insurability.
Three ownership types of non-government insurer: stock companies, mutual companies and other structures (insurance exchanges, captives).

guide.heading: Stock insurance companies
points: Profit-seeking incorporated companies that aim to earn profits for shareholders and a return (policy dividends) for participating policyowners.
Most new entrants start as stock companies, raising capital by selling equity to shareholders.

No assessable policies: if losses exceed premium revenue, shareholders absorb the shortfall through lower dividends and/or capital, so the policyowner's cost is fixed at the start. Today even mutuals rarely issue assessable policies.
Greater access to capital markets (they can issue new shares) gives stock insurers more capacity for expansion and growth than mutuals.

guide.heading: Mutual companies and their variations
points: A mutual is owned by its policyowners: buying a policy makes you a part owner. Manulife, Sun Life and Mutual Life (Clarica) began as mutuals but by 2000 had all moved to stock form to reach capital markets.

Assessment mutual (the original pure form): the cost is not fixed at the outset but set during or at the end of the term from actual experience. Small local Farm Fire companies still work this way, with low overhead.
Factory mutual: grew out of fire prevention and now covers all risks. A premium deposit funds losses, expenses and reserves, and any surplus is credited to renewal or returned.
Stock mutual: began as an assessment mutual; a provincial Act lets it sell participating policies to the public. Its policyholders are not members in the way pure assessment mutual policyowners are.
Co-operative stock mutual: capital comes from member shareholders who are also the insureds. It operates much like a stock company and usually stays within its home province.

guide.heading: Mutualization, demutualization and what clients should care about
points: Mutualization (stock to mutual) was used by troubled stock insurers to avoid insolvency, takeover or foreign control. It needs Minister of Finance permission and a by-law approved by a majority of shareholders at a special general meeting. Rare today.

Demutualization (mutual to stock) is the trend: the four pillars have blurred, so mutuals need capital to compete with banks and trust companies, and the Insurance Companies Act (1992) made it easier and let mutuals issue preferred stock and subordinate debentures.
Process: value the company on its surplus, issue common stock and give free shares to participating policyowners, who keep their insurance and cash values.
Staying mutual blocks hostile takeovers (mutuals merge only by consent). Demutualizing can backfire: Mutual Life became Clarica and was bought by Sun Life in a hostile takeover.

For clients, only stock and mutual insurers really matter. A mutual gives all net profits to participating policyowners; a stock insurer must also satisfy shareholders but tends to grow more aggressively.
In Quebec, most insurers began as village mutual assistance societies that later joined to form insurance companies with provincial charters.

guide.heading: Lloyd's of London and captive insurers
points: Lloyd's is not an insurance company but an insurance exchange: its members underwrite risks through syndicates, each with an underwriter who selects risks, and each syndicate pays its share of a loss.
It began in Edward Lloyd's London coffee house (late 17th century), where merchants wrote their names under a description of a ship's risk, giving us the term underwriter.

Individual members (Names) had unlimited liability, a strong incentive to underwrite carefully that lets Lloyd's take unusual risks (a pianist's hands, a dancer's legs), though these are a small part of its business.

Losses from the late 1980s (a record US$3.14 billion in 1989) came from the market cycle, rising costs, member scandals, disasters (Hurricane Hugo, Piper Alpha) and bad underwriting. In 1993 members voted to admit corporate members with limited liability.

Pure captive: a subsidiary of a non-insurance parent that insures only the parent's risks. Association captive: owned by a trade association to insure its members (sometimes called fraternal associations).

guide.heading: Selling property/casualty insurance
points: Clients should deal with a fully licensed agent, preferably with a financial planning designation. Insurers are regulated under the Superintendent of Financial Institutions; check stability in annual reports or with a rating firm such as Standard & Poor's.
Broker: places business with many insurers, represents the insured (not the insurer) and owns expirations, so can move the client to another insurer at renewal.
Agent: may represent only one company, either as an independent or as an employee/captive agent of a direct writer (e.g., Co-operators, Allstate). Typically does not own expirations.

Direct marketing (1-800 centres, mailings, TV/radio, the Internet, credit card tie-ins) has no intermediary and pays no commissions, so it costs less. It may be stand-alone or followed up by telemarketing.
Direct channels suit commodity products (home, auto, accidental death) but not complex ones (whole life, universal life). Many insurers combine methods.

guide.heading: Selling life and health insurance
points: Same channels: agents (life underwriters), brokers and direct marketing. Quebec was once the only province letting an agent represent more than one company; multi-insurer agents, called brokers, are now common.

Single company representation (SCR): the agent must place business with the insurer that sponsors the licence. Strictness varies; small insurers without a sales force accept business from any agent, often with high commissions.
Pay: commission (by product type and total volume; more volume means a higher rate on all business) plus quality standards, measured mainly by persistency.

General agencies represent several insurers and give agents admin, marketing and specialist support in place of a career agency system. Insurers pay them override commissions that often do not reduce agents' commissions.
In Quebec, brokerage agencies are called brokerage firms. They may represent one insurer but more typically several, and many are interdisciplinary (life, disability, group and P&C).

guide.heading: Insurer solvency and Assuris limits
points: Regulation targets insurer solvency, consumer protection (including rates) and accessibility. Solvency is the ability to meet current liabilities as they come due.
Why monitor solvency: buyers pay in advance for future benefits, and insurance is meant to reduce uncertainty, so a failure (e.g., Confederation Life) has the opposite effect.
Assuris (formerly CompCorp) protects Canadian citizens and residents who bought from a member life insurer: policies move to a solvent insurer and are protected up to set limits.
Course figures: death benefit, higher of $200,000 or 85%; cash surrender or annuity value, higher of $60,000 or 85%; health expense, critical illness, travel and seg funds, higher of $60,000 or 85%.
Income benefits (disability, long-term care, annuities, RRIF payments): higher of $2,000 a month or 85%. Accumulation annuities, including RRSPs and TFSAs held in them: up to $100,000.

Group coverage is protected like individual policies, but only until the earlier of the next group renewal or six months after the failure. Seg funds with income guarantees: $60,000/85% while saving, $2,000 a month/85% once withdrawals start.

guide.heading: Applying the Assuris limits
points: Assuris pays only the gap between what the failed insurer pays and the Assuris limit; it does not guarantee the full amount.
Course example: the insurer pays 70% of a $200,000 death benefit ($140,000) and Assuris adds $60,000. On $250,000, the insurer pays $175,000 and Assuris $37,500, for $212,500 (85%).
Death benefit limits apply per life insured with any one insurer: two $200,000 policies on the same life get at most $340,000 (85%) combined.
Cash and annuity value limits apply per policyowner, and registered and non-registered policies on the same life are treated separately.

Assuris is like CDIC for banks, but it is a non-government corporation funded by member insurers and is not federally guaranteed. P&C claimants are protected by the Property and Casualty Insurance Compensation Corporation.

guide.heading: Consumer protection and who regulates
points: Three sources of consumer protection: consumer knowledge (insurers must give adequate information), fairness of rates and insurance accessibility.

Rate regulation aims for rates that are adequate but not excessive. Not all lines are rate-regulated; mandatory auto insurance draws the most pressure, but rates set too low raise the risk of insurer insolvency.

Accessibility: the Facility Association, an unincorporated non-profit association of insurers, provides auto insurance to drivers who would otherwise struggle to get it. Insuring all HIV-positive applicants at standard rates could erode solvency.
Three broad categories of regulators: governments, courts and industry associations.

Federal law focuses on the financial soundness and solvency of federally incorporated and foreign insurers (most insurance in force). Provinces regulate provincial insurers the same way, through their Superintendent of Insurance, and regulate contracts and local business.
Courts shape practice through their decisions. In Quebec, the courts mainly interpret the law; in the common-law provinces they also take part in creating it.

guide.heading: Self-regulation, charters and licensing
points: The industry prefers self-regulation. Advocis (formerly CAIFA, before that LUAC) is a national association that works to improve the industry and flag areas needing legislation.
In Quebec, the AMF provides the self-regulation role for life/disability and P&C insurance, protecting the public by overseeing the Act respecting the distribution of financial products and services.
Most insurers hold a federal charter for national reach but need a provincial licence in each province where they operate. Smaller, niche insurers may choose a provincial charter.
Quebec has a far higher share of insurance issued by provincially chartered insurers than any other province (about 35%, per the course's self-test answer).

Common-law provinces have no uniform licensing law but similar reviews: reputation, education, employment history, suitability and good-faith intent, plus a qualifying exam (life or general insurance).
In Quebec, the AMF assesses agents' and brokers' competence in insurance law, consumer law and the product line. Life agents write the life exam; P&C sellers write the general damage insurance exam.

guide.heading: Unfair trade practices and financial regulation
points: Rebating: returning part of the premium, giving non-cash incentives of more than nominal value, or cutting fees to offset commissions, as an inducement to buy. A $25 wallet given after the sale is fine; a $250 bicycle or a paid trip is not.

Twisting: getting a client to replace a policy with a similar one from another insurer to the client's detriment. Replacement is acceptable if fully disclosed and in the client's best interest. Churning: the same practice within one insurer.
Commissions may be split only with licensed agents; an unlicensed referrer may get only a fixed finder's fee unrelated to the commission (e.g., a flat $100 per referral).

In Quebec, a registrant may share commissions with other registrants (firms, independent partnerships, independent representatives) and with deposit institutions, securities dealers and advisers, real estate brokers or insurers.
Other unfair trade practices: deceptive advertising, misrepresentation, inequitable claim settlement and discrimination contrary to accepted insurance practice.
Capital rules: MCCSR (risk-based capital) for life insurers since 1992; MCT for federally regulated P&C insurers since 2003. Liquidation of an insolvent insurer is carefully regulated.
Government programs protect society's interests: federal (EI, CPP/QPP, OAS) and provincial (health care, workers' compensation). They are often funded from current annual cash flow, not reserves.

tips: EXAM TIP: Brokers represent the insured and own their expirations; agents who represent a single insurer typically do not.
EXAM TIP: Assuris (course figures): death benefit $200,000 or 85%; cash value $60,000 or 85%; income $2,000/month or 85%; accumulation $100,000.
EXAM TIP: Assuris death-benefit limits apply per life insured with one insurer; cash-value limits apply per policyowner.
EXAM TIP: Twisting replaces a policy with another insurer's to the client's detriment; churning does the same within one insurer.
EXAM TIP: A finder's fee to an unlicensed referrer must be a fixed amount, never a share of the commission earned.
DID YOU KNOW? 'Underwriter' comes from Lloyd's coffee house, where merchants wrote their names under a description of the risk.
DID YOU KNOW? Mutuals demutualize mainly to reach capital markets, but staying mutual protects them from hostile takeovers.
DID YOU KNOW? In Quebec, the AMF assesses agents and brokers, and the courts mainly interpret the law rather than help create it.
DID YOU KNOW? Per the course, only three Canadian life insurers failed in well over 100 years, and almost no policyowners lost money.

flashcards.front: Four broad categories of insurance coverage today
flashcards.back: Property, liability, accident and sickness, and life. In the early years, each company covered only one specific risk, such as fire or marine transportation.
A policy under which the insured can be charged extra premium if the insurer's actual losses exceed expectations. Stock insurers do not issue them, and today they are uncommon even among mutuals.
An insurer owned by its policyowners: buying a policy makes you a part owner. Manulife, Sun Life and Mutual Life (Clarica) began as mutuals but had moved to become stock companies by 2000.

flashcards.front: Stock mutual vs co-operative stock mutual
flashcards.back: Stock mutual: began as an assessment mutual; a provincial Act lets it sell participating policies to the public. Co-operative stock mutual: capital comes from member shareholders who are also the insureds; usually stays in its home province.

1) The four pillars blurred, so mutuals need capital to compete with banks and trust companies. 2) The Insurance Companies Act (1992) made it easier and let mutuals issue preferred stock and subordinate debentures.

flashcards.front: Why a mutual might choose to stay mutual
flashcards.back: A mutual can merge with another mutual by common consent but cannot be bought out by a stock company in an unfriendly takeover. Mutual Life demutualized as Clarica and was taken over by Sun Life.

flashcards.front: Origin of most Quebec insurance companies
flashcards.back: Mutual assistance societies formed in small villages to protect residents, which later joined together to form insurance companies with provincial charters.

An insurance exchange, not an insurance company. Members (individual Names with unlimited liability and corporate members with limited liability, admitted after a 1993 vote) underwrite risks through syndicates; business comes through brokers worldwide.

Pure captive: insurance subsidiary of a non-insurance parent that insures only its parent's risks. Association captive: owned by a trade association to insure its members (sometimes called fraternal associations).

flashcards.front: Broker vs agent: who owns the expirations?
flashcards.back: Broker: places business with many insurers, represents the insured and owns expirations (can move the client at renewal). A single-company agent, whether independent or a direct writer's captive agent, typically does not.

The agent is contractually required to place business with the company that sponsors his or her licence. Strictness varies; small insurers without a sales force accept business from any agent or broker.

An independent sales operation, usually representing several insurers, that gives agents admin, marketing and specialist support. Insurers pay it override commissions, often without reducing agents' commissions.

flashcards.front: Assuris limits for life insurance (course figures)
flashcards.back: Death benefit: the higher of $200,000 or 85%. Cash surrender or annuity value: the higher of $60,000 or 85%.

flashcards.front: Assuris limits for income benefits (course figures)
flashcards.back: Disability, long-term care, annuity and RRIF payments: the higher of $2,000 a month or 85% of the monthly income benefit.

flashcards.front: Assuris limits for accumulation and other products (course figures)
flashcards.back: Accumulation annuities, and RRSPs, RRIFs or TFSAs held in them: up to $100,000 of accumulated value. Health expense, critical illness, travel and segregated funds: the higher of $60,000 or 85%.
The same as for individual policies, but it ends at the earlier of the group contract's next renewal date or six months after the insurer fails.

Death benefits: per life insured with any one insurer. Cash and annuity values: per policyowner. Registered and non-registered policies on the same life: treated separately. Assuris pays only the gap up to its limit.
Assuris does for life insurance what CDIC does for bank deposits, but it is a non-government corporation funded by member insurers and is not federally guaranteed.
Consumer knowledge (insurers must provide adequate information), fairness of rates (adequate but not excessive) and insurance accessibility.

flashcards.front: Three broad categories of insurance regulation
flashcards.back: Governments (federal and provincial), courts, and industry associations (self-regulation).

flashcards.front: Role of the courts: Quebec vs common-law provinces
flashcards.back: In Quebec, the courts' primary role is to interpret the law, so their influence is smaller. In the common-law provinces, the courts also take part, to some extent, in creating the law.

Provides the self-regulation role for Quebec's insurance industry (life/disability and P&C), oversees the Act respecting the distribution of financial products and services and assesses agents' and brokers' competence.
A national industry association (formerly CAIFA, and before that the Life Underwriters Association of Canada, LUAC) that works to improve the industry and identify areas that may require legislation.
Returning part of the premium, giving non-cash incentives of more than nominal value, or reducing fees to offset commissions, as an inducement to buy. Prohibited in most provinces.

Twisting: inducing a client to replace a policy with a similar one from a different insurer, to the client's detriment. Churning: the same practice when the old and new policies come from the same insurer.

flashcards.front: Commission splitting and finder's fees (most provinces)
flashcards.back: Commissions may be split only with licensed agents. An unlicensed referrer may receive a finder's fee only if it is a fixed amount not related to the commission earned.

flashcards.front: Who may share commissions in Quebec
flashcards.back: A registrant may share with any other registrant (firm, independent partnership, independent representative) and with a deposit institution, securities dealer, securities adviser, real estate broker or insurer.
MCCSR (minimum continuing capital and surplus requirements): risk-based capital for life insurers since 1992. MCT (minimum capital test): for federally regulated P&C insurers since 2003.

flashcards.front: Federal vs provincial government insurance programs
flashcards.back: Federal: Employment Insurance, CPP/QPP and Old Age Security. Provincial: mainly health care and workers' compensation. Public programs are often funded from current annual cash flow rather than reserves.

questions.q: Over time, the many separate lines of risk coverage have melded into four broad categories. Which list names them?
options: Fire, marine, automobile, and accident and sickness
Property, casualty, annuities, and life and health
Property, liability, accident and sickness, and life
Life, health, travel, and credit and mortgage
questions.explain: The course says coverage has melded into four broad categories: property, liability, accident and sickness, and life. In the early years each insurer covered only one specific risk, such as fire or marine transportation.

questions.q: Stock insurance companies do not issue assessable policies, so the policyowner's cost is fixed at the start of the policy period.
options: True
False
questions.explain: True. If a stock insurer's losses exceed its premium revenue, shareholders absorb the shortfall through lower dividends and/or capital; policyowners are not assessed. Today even mutuals rarely issue assessable policies.

questions.q: How do new entrants to the insurance industry generally get started?
options: As stock companies, capitalized by selling equity to shareholders
As mutual companies, capitalized by selling participating policies
As assessment mutuals, capitalized by assessing their members
As captive insurers, capitalized by loans from a parent company
questions.explain: New entrants generally start as stock companies, raising capital by selling equity to shareholders. That access to capital markets also gives stock insurers more capacity for expansion and growth than mutuals.

questions.q: Under a pure assessment mutual, when is the cost of the coverage determined?
options: At issue, when a level premium is fixed for the whole policy period
At each renewal, based on the average experience of all Canadian insurers
Only on dissolution, when any surplus is shared among the members
During the term or at its end, according to actual operating experience
questions.explain: With an assessment mutual, the cost is not fixed when the contract is made; it is set during the term or at its end from actual operating experience. Some small local Farm Fire companies in Canada still work this way.

questions.q: Which type of insurer charges a premium deposit to fund losses, expenses and reserves, then credits any surplus toward renewal or returns it to the policyholder?
options: A stock mutual
A factory mutual
A pure captive
A co-operative stock mutual
questions.explain: Factory mutuals grew out of fire prevention and now cover all types of risk. Losses, expenses and reserves are funded from the premium deposit plus investment income, and any surplus becomes a renewal credit or a refund.

questions.q: A struggling stock insurer wants to convert into a mutual company. What does the Insurance Act require?
options: Assuris approval and a vote of two-thirds of the participating policyowners
Minister of Finance permission and a by-law approved by a majority of shareholders
A plan filed with the provincial Superintendent of Insurance, with no vote
A surplus-based valuation and free common shares given to participating policyowners
questions.explain: Mutualization requires applying to the Minister of Finance, with the conversion plan set out in a by-law approved by a majority of shareholders at a special general meeting. Valuing on surplus and issuing free shares describes demutualization.

questions.q: As the four pillars of financial services blur, a large mutual life insurer needs more capital to compete with banks and trust companies. Which move would give it direct access to capital markets?
options: Mutualizing under the Insurance Act
Setting up a pure captive subsidiary
Converting into an assessment mutual
Demutualizing and issuing common stock
questions.explain: Demutualizing turns a mutual into a stock company that can issue shares, the main reason mutuals convert. The Insurance Companies Act of 1992 made demutualization easier and also let mutuals issue preferred stock and subordinate debentures.

questions.q: A small mutual insurer wants to remain independent. Which feature of staying mutual best supports that goal?
options: It cannot be bought out by a stock company in an unfriendly takeover
It can merge with any stock insurer without needing anyone's consent
Its policies get higher Assuris protection limits than a stock insurer's
It can raise new capital more easily by issuing common shares
questions.explain: A mutual can merge with another mutual by common consent but cannot be taken over in a hostile bid. Demutualizing can backfire: Mutual Life became Clarica and was then bought by Sun Life in a hostile takeover.

questions.q: From a participating policyowner's point of view, what is the main investment-return difference between a mutual and a stock insurer?
options: A mutual guarantees its policy dividends, while a stock insurer cannot
A stock insurer must pay policyowners first and shareholders only last
A mutual allocates all net profits to its participating policyowners
A stock insurer grows more slowly, so its policy dividends are steadier
questions.explain: A mutual has no shareholders, so all net profits can go to participating policyowners, giving it the potential to pay higher returns. A stock insurer must satisfy both groups, though it tends to grow more aggressively thanks to easier access to capital.

questions.q: A Quebec client asks why so many Quebec insurers hold provincial charters. Which historical fact best explains it?
options: Quebec law long barred federally chartered insurers from selling life insurance
Lloyd's syndicates set up Quebec subsidiaries under provincial charters
Federal stock insurers mutualized to avoid foreign control and moved to Quebec
Village mutual assistance societies merged into provincially chartered insurers
questions.explain: In Quebec, most insurers began as mutual assistance societies formed in small villages to protect residents. Over the years these societies joined together to form insurance companies with provincial charters.

questions.q: A client says she insured a rare violin 'with the Lloyd's insurance company'. How should her planner describe Lloyd's?
options: A mutual insurer owned by the policyowners who buy coverage from it
A pure captive that insures only the risks of its corporate parent
An exchange whose members, not Lloyd's itself, underwrite the risks
A stock company owned by the wealthy shareholders known as Names
questions.explain: Lloyd's of London is not actually an insurance company but an insurance exchange that provides services to its members, who underwrite insurance through syndicates. Each syndicate that insures a risk pays its share of the loss.

questions.q: Why has Lloyd's been able to underwrite unusual risks such as a concert pianist's hands or a dancer's legs?
options: Members' unlimited liability pushed them to choose risks very carefully
Unusual risks make up the largest share of Lloyd's total premium income
Lloyd's losses on catastrophic risks are backed by a government guarantee
Each unusual risk is written by one syndicate that keeps the whole premium
questions.explain: Because individual members bore the full cost of bad underwriting through unlimited liability, they had strong incentives to evaluate risks carefully. Such unusual risks are actually a relatively small part of Lloyd's business.

questions.q: After heavy losses, Lloyd's members voted in 1993 to admit corporate members, who, unlike the individual Names, have limited liability.
options: True
False
questions.explain: True. Large losses (including a record US$3.14 billion in 1989) reduced the number of Names, syndicates and capital, so corporate members with limited liability were admitted to raise capital.

questions.q: A pure captive insures the risks of its non-insurance parent company and also sells coverage to other firms to spread its risk.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. A pure captive is set up explicitly to underwrite its parent's insurance and insures no other risks. Captives that write for other firms or individuals, such as association captives owned by trade associations, are other types.

questions.q: At renewal, which intermediary has the right to move a client's property insurance to a different insurer?
options: A captive agent, because agents represent the insured
A broker, because brokers own their expirations
A single-company agent, because agents own expirations
A direct writer's employee, since it controls placement
questions.explain: Ownership of expirations is the right to control where a client's insurance is placed. Brokers have it and represent the insured; agents who represent only one company, including captive agents of direct writers, typically do not.

questions.q: Direct marketing through call centres and the Internet is best suited to which kind of insurance product?
options: Complex permanent coverage such as universal life insurance
Whole life policies that need a detailed needs analysis
Commodity-type coverage such as auto or homeowners insurance
Customized group plans designed for large unionized employers
questions.explain: Direct marketing has no intermediary and pays no commissions, so it costs less, and it suits commodity products such as home, auto and accidental death coverage. It is less appropriate for complex products like whole life or universal life.

questions.q: What does single company representation (SCR) mean for a life insurance agent?
options: The agent must place business with the insurer that sponsors the licence
The agent may serve only one client family at a time within each province
The agent may hold an insurance licence in only one province at a time
The agent may sell only one product line, such as life or general insurance
questions.explain: Under SCR, agents are contractually required to place business with the company that sponsors their licence. Strictness varies: some insurers allow almost no outside placements, while others are much less restrictive.

questions.q: When insurers reward the quality of an agent's business, what is the main measure they use?
options: The number of different insurers the agent places business with
The average face amount of the policies the agent sells
The share of the agent's sales that are permanent policies
Persistency: whether clients keep or renew their policies
questions.explain: Agents are paid partly by commission (based on product type and total volume placed with an insurer) and partly for meeting quality standards. Quality is mainly measured by persistency: policies kept in force rather than lapsing.

questions.q: A general agency provides illustrations, application processing and tax specialists to the independent agents it supports. How is the general agency usually paid?
options: A fixed share deducted from each agent's commissions on placed business
Override commissions from insurers, often not cut from agents' pay
Monthly fees charged to clients for the specialist services provided
Salaries paid by the insurers whose career agency system it replaces
questions.explain: General agencies receive override commissions from insurers on the business they manage for their agents. In many cases this override comes directly from the insurer and does not reduce the commissions otherwise payable to the agent.

questions.q: In Quebec, brokerage agencies are usually called brokerage firms, and while some represent a single insurer, most represent several.
options: True
False
questions.explain: True. Quebec brokerage firms may represent one insurer but more typically represent several, and many are interdisciplinary, offering life, disability, group, and property and casualty insurance.

questions.q: Which pair of reasons explains why regulators monitor the solvency of insurers?
options: Insurers hold bank deposits, and their failures would trigger CDIC payouts
Buyers pay in advance for future benefits, and failures increase insecurity
Premiums are tax-deductible, and failures would reduce government revenue
Agents are paid in advance, and failures would cancel all of their licences
questions.explain: Consumers pay before benefits are due, so they need assurance the promise will be kept; and insurance exists to reduce uncertainty, so an insolvency has the opposite effect. The failure of Confederation Life badly shook public confidence.

questions.q: Using the course's Assuris limits, what protection applies to a life insurance death benefit?
options: The higher of $60,000 or 85% of the death benefit
The lower of $200,000 or 85% of the death benefit
Up to $100,000 of the death benefit for each policy
The higher of $200,000 or 85% of the death benefit
questions.explain: Death benefits are protected to the higher of $200,000 or 85%. The $60,000-or-85% limit applies to cash surrender values, and the $100,000 limit applies to accumulated value in accumulation annuities.

questions.q: Kim receives $3,000 a month from an annuity with a life insurer that becomes insolvent. Using the course's Assuris limits, how much monthly income is protected?
options: $2,550 a month
$2,000 a month
$3,000 a month
$1,800 a month
questions.explain: Annuity income is protected to the higher of $2,000 a month or 85% of the monthly income benefit. Here 85% × $3,000 = $2,550, which is higher than $2,000, so up to $2,550 a month is protected.

questions.q: Lena's $300,000 term policy is with an insurer that fails and can pay only 60 cents on the dollar. Using the course's Assuris rules, how much would Assuris add if Lena died?
questions.explain: The insurer pays 60%, or $180,000. Assuris protects the higher of $200,000 or 85% of $300,000 ($255,000) and pays only the gap: $255,000 − $180,000 = $75,000.

questions.q: How are Assuris limits counted for life insurance death benefits compared with cash surrender values?
options: Death benefits per policyowner; cash values per life insured with one insurer
Both per policy, so each separate contract gets its own full limit
Both per family, so spouses share a single limit for all their policies
Death benefits per life insured with one insurer; cash values per policyowner
questions.explain: The $200,000 death-benefit maximum is computed per life insured with any one insurer, so two policies on the same life share it. Cash and annuity value limits are computed per policyowner, so each owner gets a separate limit.

questions.q: An RRSP accumulation annuity and a non-registered deferred annuity on the same person's life, with the same failed insurer, share a single $100,000 Assuris limit.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. For cash value guarantees, registered and non-registered policies on the same life are treated as separate entities, so each is protected up to the $100,000 accumulated-value limit (course figure).

questions.q: The course names three sources of consumer protection in the insurance market. Which list is correct?
options: Governments, the courts and industry self-regulation associations
Assuris, the Facility Association and provincial rate review boards
Consumer knowledge, fairness of rates and insurance accessibility
Solvency testing, rate freezes and compulsory automobile coverage
questions.explain: Consumer protection comes from consumer knowledge (insurers must give adequate information), fairness of rates (adequate but not excessive) and accessibility. Governments, courts and industry associations are the three categories of regulators.

questions.q: A driver with a poor record cannot find an insurer willing to cover his car. Which body exists to provide auto insurance in this situation?
options: The Facility Association
Assuris
The Property and Casualty Insurance Compensation Corporation
The Autorité des marchés financiers
questions.explain: The Facility Association is an unincorporated non-profit association of insurers that provides auto insurance to people who would otherwise have difficulty getting it. Access matters because auto insurance is mandatory for all drivers.

questions.q: Federal insurance legislation in Canada is primarily concerned with which of the following?
options: Licensing the agents and brokers who sell insurance in each province
The financial soundness and solvency of federal and foreign insurers
Regulating the insurance contract and sales practices in each province
Setting automobile insurance rates for drivers in every province
questions.explain: Federal legislation focuses on the financial soundness and solvency of federally incorporated and foreign insurers, which underwrite most insurance in force. Provinces regulate contracts, licensing and the business of insurance within their borders.

questions.q: How does the role of the courts in Quebec differ from their role in the common-law provinces?
options: Quebec courts create insurance law; common-law courts only interpret statutes
Quebec courts license insurance agents; common-law courts discipline them
Quebec courts mainly interpret the law; common-law courts also help create it
Quebec courts hear no insurance disputes, which all go to the AMF instead
questions.explain: In Quebec, the courts' primary role is to interpret the law, so their influence is less important than in the common-law provinces, where courts also participate, to a certain extent, in creating the law.

questions.q: Chloé lives in Laval and wants to become licensed to sell life insurance. Which body assesses her competence, and which exam must she write?
options: The AMF; the life insurance exam
The AMF; the general damage insurance exam
Advocis; the life insurance exam
The Superintendent of Insurance; a general exam
questions.explain: In Quebec, the Autorité des marchés financiers assesses the competence of agents and brokers. Life agents write the life insurance exam; those who want to sell property or liability insurance write an exam on general damage insurance.

questions.q: A federally chartered insurer plans to sell policies in four provinces. What else does it need?
options: Nothing more, since a federal charter applies across Canada
A second charter under each province's business corporations act
A separate Assuris membership for each province where it sells
A provincial licence from each province in which it operates
questions.explain: Most insurers are federally chartered for national market potential, but they still need a provincial licence in each province where they operate. These licences also regulate cross-border sales and agents' and brokers' selling jurisdictions.

questions.q: Compared with the other provinces, what is distinctive about the insurance issued in Quebec?
options: Almost all of it is issued by federally chartered foreign insurers
A much larger share is issued by provincially chartered insurers
Most of it is sold by direct marketing rather than through firms
Most of it is underwritten by Lloyd's syndicates through brokers
questions.explain: A significant amount of Quebec insurance is issued by insurers with a Quebec charter, a much higher share than in any other province; the course's self-test answer puts it at about 35%.

questions.q: Which of these client gifts would be acceptable under the rules against rebating?
options: A $250 gift card for each client who buys a juvenile policy from her
A $25 policy wallet handed to each client after the sale is completed
A paid ski weekend for clients who place $10,000 of commission business
A cash refund of part of the first premium, paid from her commission
questions.explain: A low-value item given after the sale is not an inducement to buy, so it is not rebating. Returning part of the premium, or giving valuable incentives such as gift cards or trips tied to a purchase, is rebating.

questions.q: An agent keeps persuading clients to replace their policies with new, similar policies issued by the same insurer, to the clients' detriment. What is this practice called?
options: Twisting
Rebating
Commission splitting
Churning
questions.explain: Churning is twisting where the replaced and replacement policies are issued by the same company. Twisting is replacing a policy with a similar one from a different insurer to the client's detriment.

questions.q: When is it acceptable for an agent to recommend that a client replace a life policy with a similar one from another insurer?
options: When it rests on accurate, fully disclosed facts and serves the client's interest
When the new policy pays the agent a lower commission than the old policy did
Never, since replacing a policy with another insurer's is always twisting
Only if the replacement is issued by the same insurer as the original policy
questions.explain: Replacement is improper twisting only when it harms the client. It is acceptable if based on accurate, fully disclosed information and in the client's best interest, supported by a complete financial comparison.

questions.q: Lucie, a licensed life agent in Ontario, gets client referrals from an unlicensed accountant. Which payment arrangement is permitted?
options: 10% of every commission Lucie earns from each referred client
$100 per referral, rising to $300 if the client buys a large policy
A flat $100 per referral, whether or not Lucie makes a sale
Half of Lucie's first-year commission on any policy a referral buys
questions.explain: Commissions may be split only with licensed agents. An unlicensed person may receive a finder's fee, but it must be a fixed amount not related to the commission earned, so any fee that grows with the sale is improper.

questions.q: In Quebec, a registrant under the Act respecting the distribution of financial products and services wants to share a commission. Which of these may receive a share?
options: A notary who referred the client
An unregistered accountant
The client's employer
A real estate broker
questions.explain: In Quebec, a registrant may share commissions with any other registrant (firm, independent partnership or independent representative) and with a deposit institution, securities dealer, securities adviser, real estate broker or insurer.

questions.q: The minimum capital test (MCT) introduced in 2003 sets the risk-based capital requirements for life insurance companies.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. MCT guidelines (2003) apply to federally regulated property and casualty insurers. Life insurers have been subject to the minimum continuing capital and surplus requirements (MCCSR) since 1992.

questions.q: How does the funding of public insurance programs usually differ from that of private insurers?
options: Public programs are fully funded by reserves invested in capital markets
Public programs are funded by Assuris contributions from member insurers
Public programs are often funded from current annual cash flow, not reserves
Public programs are funded by assessing participants after each year has ended
questions.explain: Private insurance is reserve-driven, while public programs (EI, CPP/QPP and OAS federally; health care and workers' compensation provincially) are often funded from current annual cash flow: premiums received and claims paid.

questions.q: Alfred trusts banks because of CDIC coverage but fears his money is unprotected with a life insurer. What should his planner tell him?
options: Assuris protects policyowners up to set limits if a member insurer fails
CDIC also guarantees life insurance cash values up to $100,000 per insurer
The federal government guarantees all life insurance policies in full
There is no protection, so he should keep all his savings in a bank
questions.explain: Assuris, the industry-funded plan, protects policyowners of member insurers up to set limits, e.g. $100,000 of accumulated value, $60,000 of cash value and $200,000 or 85% of death benefits (course figures). Unlike CDIC, it is not government-guaranteed.
